title: Secrets Done Right: From a Leaked Key to Credentials That Expire on Their Own
intro: Most breaches start with a credential: a key committed to Git, a password shared by ten services, a token that never expires. This path follows a team cleaning that up. First find the secrets you already leaked, then see why Kubernetes Secrets alone aren't the answer, then move to a vault, short-lived credentials, workload identity, and certificates, and finish with the outages that rotation can cause when it's done carelessly.
resolution: The direction of travel is the same at every step: fewer secrets, shorter lives, and identity instead of passwords. A leaked key is revoked first and cleaned up second. A Kubernetes Secret is only base64, so the source of truth moves to a vault, and from there into the cluster by an operator or encrypted in Git. Dynamic credentials and workload identity remove most long-lived secrets entirely, because nothing that expires in an hour is worth stealing for long. The two incidents are the price of rotation done in a hurry: a new password that took most of an hour to travel from Vault to a pod that only read it at startup, and a CA replaced without a period where clients trusted both. Rotation is safe when the old and new are both valid for a while. Next, write the policy yourself in the Vault and cert-manager Writing Labs.
